findings.claim: “In textbooks you will also see these called anticlines and synclines when geologists know which beds are older; for your exam, antiform and synform are the precise terms for geometry alone.” The same paragraph defines antiform and synform by the age of the core rocks.
findings.truth: Antiform and synform are defined by the direction of closure, not by age. Anticline and syncline are the age-based terms. The lesson defines antiform by age and then tells the student the term is for geometry alone, so it contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: spec 1.5 (folded beds [antiform, synform, axial plane trace, limb]); standard structural-geology definitions.

findings.claim: “Never confuse dip (angle) with strike (compass direction) — examiners report this as a common error.”
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited or available. Claims about what examiner reports say must not be invented.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: Q4 asks the student to “calculate the vertical drop in elevation across this traverse” after walking “400 m perpendicular to strike along the surface”.
findings.truth: The mark scheme computes 400 × tan(35°) = 280 m, which is the vertical drop of the BED over a 400 m HORIZONTAL distance, not a change in ground elevation. Recomputed: tan 35° = 0.7002, 400 × 0.7002 = 280.1 m, so the key is right but the stem asks for the wrong quantity.
findings.evidence: recomputation.

findings.claim: “A distinctive feature is that the rock sequence is repeated on either side of the fault” — given as the map signature of a NORMAL fault.
findings.truth: Reversed relationship. Repetition of a succession is diagnostic of reverse and thrust faulting (compressional shortening). A normal fault cuts beds OUT of the succession; on a map it exposes younger rocks on the downthrown side and older rocks on the upthrown side.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Fault (geology) — “Reverse faults indicate compressive shortening of the crust”; standard map-interpretation criterion.

findings.claim: “In a diagram, check: if the rocks on the left side of the fault appear to have moved upward, the left block is the hanging wall and it has gone up — reverse fault.”
findings.truth: Which block is the hanging wall depends on the dip of the fault plane, not on which side of the page it sits or on which side moved up. If the left block is the footwall and it has moved up, the hanging wall has moved down and the fault is normal. The rule as written gives the wrong answer half the time.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Fault (geology) — hanging wall is the block above the fault plane.

findings.claim: “When the fault plane is very shallow — dipping at less than 30° — the structure is specifically called a thrust fault”, while reverse faults are said to dip “at 45° or more”. Repeated in practice Q4 and a flashcard.
findings.truth: The convention is that a thrust fault is a reverse fault dipping at 45° or less. The lesson leaves 30–45° unclassified between its two definitions.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Thrust fault — “A thrust fault is a type of reverse fault that has a dip of 45 degrees or less.”

findings.claim: “Examiner reports consistently flag this mix-up.”
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: “Missing the comparison word (whereas/while/by contrast) is the most common reason students score 2 out of 4.”
findings.truth: An invented statistic about candidate performance. No such data exists in any published source.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: “the Pacific Plate moves north-west past the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year”.
findings.truth: Pacific–North America relative motion is about 5 cm per year; the San Andreas Fault itself takes up only 2–3.5 cm per year of it. 6 cm per year is too high.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, San Andreas Fault — fault slip rate 20–35 mm/yr; plate-boundary slippage 33–37 mm/yr across California.

findings.claim: Q5 is labelled “Calculate (Maths Skill)”, gives a map scale of 1:25,000 and states the dyke is “displaced 200 m”; the mark scheme then admits “already given as actual distance in this example”.
findings.truth: There is nothing to calculate: the answer is in the stem and the scale cannot be used. The stem must give a map distance so the scale conversion is real.
findings.evidence: recomputation: 8 mm on a 1:25,000 map = 8 × 25,000 = 200,000 mm = 200 m.

findings.claim: “A cross-section in your textbook or on the the practical-skills component map”.
findings.truth: Duplicated article: “the the”.
findings.evidence: reading.

findings.claim: “At which Scottish coastal site did James Hutton first describe a famous angular unconformity?”
findings.truth: Siccar Point (1788) was not Hutton's first unconformity. He had already described unconformities at Jedburgh and on Arran in 1787. Siccar Point is his most famous one, not his first.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Siccar Point — boat trip in 1788; Hutton's earlier 1787 Jedburgh and Arran observations.

findings.claim: “the principle of gradualism (also called uniformitarianism)”.
findings.truth: They are not the same idea. Uniformitarianism is the principle that the present is the key to the past. Gradualism is the claim that change is slow and continuous. The spec lists them separately, so a student who defines uniformitarianism as “slow change” can lose the mark.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2b (catastrophism v gradualism) and spec 2.3a (“uniformitarianism - the present is the key to the past”).

findings.claim: “In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the hypothesis of continental drift.”
findings.truth: The spec dates continental drift to Wegener (1915), the year of his book. 1912 is the year of his first lectures and papers. Giving only 1912 conflicts with the date the exam uses.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2d — “Continental drift was proposed by Wegener (1915)”.

findings.claim: “the three features of magnetic stripe patterns that examiners say students miss” and “Examiner reports flag missing any of these three features as the most common error on magnetic stripes questions.”
findings.truth: Two fabricated examiner claims in one lesson.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims.

findings.claim: “The Pacific Plate moves north-west relative to the Australian Plate at about 7 cm per year.”
findings.truth: Wrong frame of reference. Relative to the Australian Plate the Pacific Plate moves roughly westwards, not north-west. About 7 cm per year north-west is the Pacific Plate's absolute motion (7–11 cm/yr, from the Hawaiian hotspot track), so the rate is fine once the Australian Plate is removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Pacific Plate — moving north-west at 7–11 cm per year.

findings.claim: “The Mid-Atlantic Ridge... extends from the Arctic Ocean to near the tip of South Africa.”
findings.truth: The ridge runs south to the Bouvet Triple Junction at about 55°S, some 20 degrees of latitude further south than the Cape.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Mid-Atlantic Ridge — Gakkel Ridge junction to the Bouvet Triple Junction.

findings.claim: “the Pacific Plate slides north-west relative to the North American Plate at roughly 5–6 cm per year”.
findings.truth: Same error as F9. About 5 cm per year is the accepted relative plate motion.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, San Andreas Fault — 33–37 mm/yr across California; fault slip 20–35 mm/yr.

findings.claim: “The Mariana Trench in the Pacific reaches over 11,000 m depth.”
findings.truth: The accepted maximum depth of the Challenger Deep is 10,935 ± 6 m (2021), with earlier surveys between 10,920 m and 10,994 m. It is just under 11,000 m, not over it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Challenger Deep — 10,935 ± 6 m (2021); 10,920 ± 10 m (GEBCO 1993).

findings.claim: “The depth of earthquake foci in the Benioff zone increases with distance from the trench, allowing geologists to infer the dip angle of the subducting slab using seismic tomography.”
findings.truth: The dip of the slab is read from the pattern of earthquake foci themselves. Seismic tomography is a separate technique that images velocity anomalies; it is not how the Benioff zone dip is measured.
findings.evidence: internal logic of the sentence; spec 2.2f (Benioff zone) and 2.2g (seismic tomography) list them separately.

findings.claim: “For the 6-mark QER, examiners expect you to name at least three pieces of evidence...”
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim, and it asserts a mark tariff the spec never states.
findings.evidence: spec assessment summary gives only component length, weighting and total marks (80 each); house rule on examiner claims.

findings.claim: The asthenosphere is defined as “the weak, partially molten zone in the upper mantle” in the dfn attribute, the glossary and a flashcard, while the body text says only that it is “slightly weaker and more ductile”.
findings.truth: The asthenosphere is solid but ductile; any melt fraction is under about one per cent. The spec calls it a “weaker layer composed of upper mantle” and says nothing about melt. Options: (a) leave it, since “partially molten” is printed in many GCSE textbooks; (b) change all three places to “weak, ductile”, matching the spec wording and the lesson's own body text. I recommend (b) — three surgical edits, and it removes an internal contradiction.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2b — asthenosphere [weaker layer composed of upper mantle].
findings.ruling: Leave: partially-molten wording is the textbook simplification; labels kept.

findings.claim: Every lesson labels its last question “6 marks — Extended Response (QER)” and uses the band names Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging.
findings.truth: The spec never uses the term QER, never states a per-question tariff, and never publishes band names for this qualification. It states only: on-screen paper 1 h 15 min, 80 marks, 50%; written paper 1 h 30 min, 80 marks, 50%, wholly based on a simplified geological map; a data sheet in both; untiered. Options: (a) keep the labels (QER is house shorthand used across the site and WJEC does use the term in other subjects); (b) relabel all six as “6 marks — Extended Response”. I recommend (a) for the type labels, with the in-prose tariff claim already removed by F21.
findings.evidence: spec lines 106–129 and 254–275; grep for “QER”, “tier” and “SPaG” in the spec returns nothing.
findings.ruling: Leave: partially-molten wording is the textbook simplification; labels kept.

findings.claim: Lesson 3 (102 characters), lesson 4 (114) and lesson 6 (102) have descriptions longer than 100 characters.
findings.truth: Pre-existing, not a factual error, but it is the validator's description limit. Flagged so the applier is not surprised if the unit-wide check trips.
findings.evidence: character count.

findings.claim: No lesson in the unit states the rule of Vs, dip and strike of outcrops crossing valleys, plunge, the Moho, or P and S wave behaviour and the S-wave shadow zone.
findings.truth: Nothing wrong is said about any of these. The earlier rule-of-Vs inversion found in this subject is not present in this unit — there is no statement of the rule to invert. Recorded only so the gap is not mistaken for a clean check.
findings.evidence: grep of all six raw lessons for “rule of V”, “up-valley”, “upstream”, “downstream” returns nothing.

summary: Two HIGH errors, both in lesson 2: repetition of strata is given as the map signature of a normal fault (it is diagnostic of reverse and thrust faults), and the hanging wall is identified by which side of the diagram moved up rather than by the dip of the fault plane. Five fabricated examiner claims across lessons 1, 2, 5 and 6, two broken or ambiguous 'calculate' questions, the thrust-fault dip convention, the Wegener date against the spec, and four wrong values (Pacific plate rates ×2, Mariana Trench depth, Mid-Atlantic Ridge extent) make up the rest. No board name appears anywhere in the unit and no lesson claims tiers, SPaG marks or another board's paper structure.
